entries.sentence: Parents may notice wheezing, cough or a tight chest; diagnosis can take time, and the NHS says call 999 if the reliever is not helping.
entries.note: NHS and Asthma and Lung UK: call 999 if the reliever is not helping; symptoms list from NHS; diagnosis time per NHS.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness as the main signs of asthma, and they usually come and go.
entries.note: NHS summary.

entries.sentence: Diagnosis can take time because symptoms vary, and testing is difficult in young children, so a trial of asthma medicines may be used.
entries.note: As body section 2.

entries.sentence: Reliever inhalers are used when needed and preventer inhalers every day; children who use an inhaler are advised to use a spacer.
entries.note: As body section 4.

entries.sentence: Every child with asthma should have a written asthma action plan and a review at least once a year.
entries.note: Charity and NHS.

entries.sentence: Call 999 for an asthma attack that the reliever inhaler does not control; contact the GP the same day when symptoms are worsening.
entries.note: As body section 7.

entries.sentence: Asthma is a common long-term condition in which the airways are inflamed and sensitive.
entries.note: NHS pages describe asthma as a common long-term condition with inflamed, sensitive airways.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness as the main signs, and they often flare at night or early in the morning.
entries.note: Main signs and night/early-morning pattern, per search summary of NHS asthma page.

entries.sentence: Wheezing is a whistling sound when a child breathes, and a dry cough that does not go away, especially at night or after exercise, is also on the NHS list.
entries.note: Healthier Together (NHS) wording: wheezing a whistling sound; dry cough that does not go away especially at night or after exercise.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK says younger children may complain of a tummy ache, lose their appetite, say their ribs ache or seem more tired than usual.
entries.note: Charity page lists tummy ache, lost appetite, ribs ache, more tired than normal.

entries.sentence: The NHS says these symptoms usually come and go.
entries.note: NHS asthma summary: symptoms usually come and go.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK suggests a visit to the GP if a child needs the blue reliever inhaler three or more times a week, wakes at night coughing or wheezing, struggles with exercise, or misses school because of asthma.
entries.note: Charity list of reasons to see the GP (number stated in returned text). Routine GP route.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a GP or nurse usually asks questions and listens to the chest.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis summary.

entries.sentence: A simple breathing test may also be used, and the NHS names spirometry and peak flow tests as the main ones.
entries.note: NHS summary: breathing tests, spirometry and peak flow main ones.

entries.sentence: Asthma can take time to diagnose because the symptoms often change over time.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS page: can take some time to diagnose because symptoms vary over time.

entries.sentence: Guidance used by the NHS says a diagnosis should be confirmed once a child is able to manage lung function tests.
entries.note: Returned text: diagnosis confirmed when child able to undergo objective testing; Right Decisions page covers objective tests from age 5 to 16.

entries.sentence: In children under 5, that testing is difficult, and spirometry is not practical for this age group.
entries.note: Returned summary: diagnosis challenging in under 5s, objective testing difficult, spirometry not feasible.

entries.sentence: Wheezing is common in many other chest conditions, and most children whose wheezing comes with viral infections stop wheezing as they get older and do not develop asthma.
entries.note: Returned summary of NHS pathways: wheeze common in other respiratory conditions; most viral-induced wheeze stops.

entries.sentence: For young children who cannot do lung function tests, a clinician may suggest a trial of asthma medicines.
entries.note: Trial of asthma medicines for children unable to do lung function tests.

entries.sentence: NICE guidance, written with the British Thoracic Society and SIGN, describes this trial as part of reaching a diagnosis, with a review afterwards to see whether symptoms return.
entries.note: NG245 summary: empirical treatment trial, then review; if symptoms recur diagnosis considered confirmed. Duration and dose deliberately left out.

entries.sentence: The pathway also notes that getting better on treatment is not proof of asthma, because wheezing caused by a virus can settle on its own.
entries.note: Returned text: improvement on treatment is not proof of asthma as viral wheeze can remit.

entries.sentence: A trigger is something that makes asthma symptoms flare up.
entries.note: Plain definition.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK lists colds and viruses, exercise, weather changes, smoke and pollution, strong emotions, and allergens such as pollen, dust mites, pets or mould.
entries.note: Trigger list from returned summaries of charity and Healthier Together pages.

entries.sentence: It describes colds and viruses as the most common cause of flare-ups.
entries.note: Colds and viruses - the most common cause of asthma flare-ups.

entries.sentence: Every child has their own set of triggers, and it helps to record them in the asthma plan.
entries.note: Everyone with asthma has own triggers; helpful to record in asthma plan.

entries.sentence: Keeping a diary of symptoms and triggers, in a notebook or on a phone, can help families spot them.
entries.note: Charity suggests a diary of symptoms and triggers.

entries.sentence: The NHS says there is not currently enough evidence to know whether suspected causes such as genetics and pollution actually cause asthma.
entries.note: Returned summary of NHS page on causes.

entries.sentence: The NHS says inhalers are the mainstay of treatment, with tablets or other treatments used if inhalers are not enough.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary.

entries.sentence: A reliever inhaler is used when needed to relieve symptoms quickly for a short time.
entries.note: Reliever description.

entries.sentence: A preventer inhaler is used every day to stop symptoms happening.
entries.note: Preventer description.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK says the preventer is used daily as prescribed, even when a child feels well.
entries.note: Returned back-to-school tip: use steroid preventer daily as prescribed even when well.

entries.sentence: One NHS page says a child who uses the reliever often will also need a preventer inhaler.
entries.note: Healthier Together: if child needs reliever more than once a day or several times a week they also need a preventer (figures left out).

entries.sentence: Children who use a metered-dose inhaler are advised to use a spacer, a device that helps the medicine get into the lungs.
entries.note: Spacer advice from Healthier Together and Asthma and Lung UK (best with pMDI).

entries.sentence: Younger children may be given their medicine through a nebuliser instead of an inhaler.
entries.note: Under-5s may be prescribed medicine through a nebuliser.

entries.sentence: An asthma action plan is a written guide made with the GP or asthma nurse.
entries.note: Written, personalised plan from GP or asthma nurse.

entries.sentence: It explains how to look after the child's asthma every day and what to do if symptoms get worse.
entries.note: Healthier Together wording.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK says every child with asthma should have one, covering daily medicines, triggers, symptoms and what to do in an attack.
entries.note: Charity: every child should have a personal asthma action plan.

entries.sentence: Many plans use green, amber and red zones.
entries.note: Returned summary mentions green, amber, red zones.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK suggests sharing the plan with the child's school or college.
entries.note: Charity advice to share plan with school.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a personal plan should be reviewed with a nurse, doctor or pharmacist at least once a year.
entries.note: NHS summary: reviewed at least once a year.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK says a child should have an asthma review at least once a year, and the GP surgery usually sends an invitation.
entries.note: Charity review page.

entries.sentence: At the review the GP or nurse typically asks about symptoms and triggers, checks how often the reliever is used, checks inhaler technique and updates the plan.
entries.note: Charity review page contents.

entries.sentence: Families do not need to wait for the review if they are worried, and can speak to the GP, nurse or pharmacist at any time.
entries.note: Charity: don't need to wait for annual review.

entries.sentence: The NHS says signs of an attack include symptoms getting worse, the reliever not helping, and being too breathless to speak, eat or sleep.
entries.note: NHS asthma attack page signs (search summary).

entries.sentence: NHS children's pages describe a child who is too breathless to talk, eat or drink, has blue lips, or is very drowsy as an emergency.
entries.note: Red/emergency signs in returned summary of NHS children's pages.

entries.sentence: Asthma and Lung UK says to call 999 if a child's reliever inhaler is not helping their symptoms or is not available.
entries.note: Charity: call 999 if reliever not helping or unavailable.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance if the person feels worse at any point, or does not improve after following the attack steps.
entries.note: NHS: if feel worse at any point or don't improve after the steps, call 999. Puff counts deliberately omitted.

entries.sentence: While waiting, the advice is to keep the child sitting up and calm, and to use a spacer with the inhaler if they have one.
entries.note: Sit up, stay calm, spacer if available.

entries.sentence: Some inhalers, known as MART inhalers, have different attack steps, so the child's own action plan applies.
entries.note: Charity notes MART inhalers differ and to check the action plan.

entries.sentence: Call 999 for an attack that the reliever inhaler does not control, or when a child cannot talk, eat or drink because of breathlessness.
entries.note: 999 route per NHS, Asthma and Lung UK and Healthier Together wording.

entries.sentence: If a child is wheezy and breathless and the reliever does not keep symptoms away for as long as the action plan expects, local NHS guidance advises contacting the GP the same day.
entries.note: Amber step: contact GP same day (interval left out).

entries.sentence: NHS 111 can give urgent advice when the GP surgery is closed.
entries.note: General NHS signposting.

entries.sentence: After an attack that led to hospital care, NHS guidance says to arrange a GP appointment within 48 hours of discharge.
entries.note: Returned summary: GP appointment within 48 hours of discharge.

entries.sentence: For symptoms that are more frequent but not urgent, a routine appointment with the GP or asthma nurse is the usual route.
entries.note: See GP or asthma nurse if symptoms recur.
